questions.question: Do I need a permit to remove a tree on my private property, how do I apply, and who reviews it? What are the fees for each tree?
questions.answer: Yes, a permit is required to remove any 'designated tree' (DBH of 8 inches or more) on private property (§273-4). Application is made in writing to the Building Inspector, who consults with the Tree Preservation Board before issuing or denying the permit (§273-7A). The application must include: applicant name/address, property address and tax map designation, total land area, number/size/species of trees, reason for removal, removal method, name of contractor, a tree survey or sketch, and proof that neighbors within 50 yards were notified at least two weeks prior (§273-7A). The Building Inspector reviews the application in consultation with the Tree Preservation Board. No permit fees per tree are specified in the provided sources. Emergency removal of an immediately threatening tree is allowed without a permit, but a written explanation must be submitted to the Building Inspector within three days (§273-11).
questions.shortAnswer: Yes; apply in writing to Building Inspector; fees not specified.
questions.gap: Gaps vs. best practice: (1) DBH threshold is 8 inches, slightly above the 6–10 inch best-practice range but within it; (2) no tiered fee structure or per-tree fees are specified; (3) no decision timeline (21–30 days) is stated; (4) neighbor notification radius is 50 yards rather than the best-practice 100 feet (actually 50 yards is ~150 feet, so this exceeds best practice); (5) no explicit surcharge for large-scale removals; (6) no exemption from fees for dead/hazardous/invasive trees is mentioned (fees not addressed at all); (7) referral threshold to Planning Board for large removals is not specified as a standalone rule (only in context of site plans/subdivisions).

questions.question: What are the penalties for removing trees without a permit?
questions.answer: Under §273-12, any person violating the chapter (including removing trees without a permit) is subject to: (A) a fine of no less than $250 and not exceeding $5,000; (B) each violation to an individual designated tree constitutes a separate offense; (C) mandatory replacement of any removed tree with a tree of the same species, size, and/or value as determined by the Building Inspector; and (D) no building permit, demolition permit, or certificate of occupancy shall be granted until all provisions of the chapter have been satisfied.
questions.gap: No imprisonment provision is specified (best practice suggests up to 30 days). The minimum fine ($250) is lower than best practice's $1,000 first-offense threshold, and there is no escalating fine structure for repeat offenses.

questions.question: Can I replant new trees to replace those removed, in lieu of a payment? Am I allowed to plant non-native species as replacements?
questions.answer: Yes, replanting is required when trees are removed. Under § 273-9, the disturbed area must be restored by backfilling, replanting and/or reseeding. Under § 273-10, any street tree removed must be replaced with new trees in the nearest practical location. The size and variety of replacement trees shall be as required by the Village — no specific native species requirement is stated, though poplar trees are prohibited within 50 feet of any sewer or sewer branch. There is no explicit provision allowing replanting in lieu of a payment, nor is there a payment-in-lieu option described. Non-native species are not explicitly prohibited (except poplars near sewers), but species selection is subject to Village approval.
questions.shortAnswer: Replanting required; species set by Village
questions.gap: The statute requires replanting but does not offer a formal payment-in-lieu option, does not require native species, does not reference an approved species list, and does not establish a dedicated tree fund for cases where on-site replanting is impractical.

questions.question: Does the code recognize the importance of keeping a healthy tree canopy?
questions.answer: Yes. §273-1 explicitly recognizes that destruction or damage to shade, ornamental, and evergreen trees causes barren conditions, increased surface drainage problems, impaired property values, and deterioration adversely affecting health, safety, environment, ecosystems, and general welfare, and the chapter seeks to correct these conditions.
questions.gap: The purpose statement recognizes tree canopy importance but the sources do not confirm specific canopy coverage targets, measurement methods, species diversity goals, tree-topping prohibitions, or replanting mandates aligned with best practices.
